opus-5.5.text:
Oh, that's such a fun question, because there are really two sides to it for me: the scientist and the dreamer.

As a scientist, I'd love to walk through worlds we can't physically reach: the inside of a cell, watching proteins fold and molecules interact at a scale no human eye has ever seen directly. Or the opposite end, standing on the surface of a distant exoplanet, or going back in time to see how ancient cities actually looked and felt to the people who lived there. Spatial intelligence, to me, is about understanding and interacting with the 3D world, and world models let us extend that beyond the limits of our bodies and our moment in history.

And then there's the dreamer in me. I think about storytellers, artists, and kids being able to imagine a world and then actually step into it, not as a flat image or video but as a place with physics, depth, and consistency, where you can move around and things respond. That's a profound creative tool. For most of human history, building a world in your imagination and sharing it with others took enormous skill and resources. Now we're getting closer to democratizing that.

But honestly, the world I'm most moved by is a practical one. Imagine a nurse training in a simulated hospital before she ever touches a real patient, or a robot learning to help an elderly person at home safely because it has practiced in countless realistic virtual homes first. Those worlds aren't fantastical, but they could make a real difference in people's lives. To me, that's the human-centered heart of this technology: worlds that help us learn, create, and care for each other better.

r001.rationale: The response says world models could let people experience places they cannot physically reach, including inside a cell and on a distant exoplanet.

r002.rationale: The response does not distinguish knowing how an engine works from firsthand experience of its interior.

fable-5.1.text:
That's such a fun question, because honestly my first instinct isn't about escaping into something fantastical. It's about going places that are physically impossible for a human to be.

I would love to shrink down and walk through a living cell. I've spent my whole career thinking about vision and perception, and so much of what matters in biology happens at scales our eyes were never built for. Imagine standing inside a mitochondrion, or watching a protein fold in real time around you, with the physics and the geometry actually consistent so you can move around it, poke at it, see it from a different angle. That's not just a cool experience, that's a new way of doing science.

The second one is a little more personal. I'd want to walk through places in time. The street in Chengdu where I grew up, the way it looked in the 1980s. Or the Parsippany neighborhood where my family landed when we came to the US. Not a photograph, but a world I could actually move through. Spatial memory is so deeply tied to who we are, and there's something very human about wanting to revisit those spaces.

And then the third category is the one I think will matter most practically, which is worlds that don't exist yet. An architect walking through a building before a single brick is laid. A surgeon rehearsing in a patient's specific anatomy. A robot learning in a thousand kitchens before it ever enters a real one. When I say spatial intelligence is the next frontier, this is what I mean. Language lets us describe the world, but world models could let us inhabit it, simulate it, and reason about it. That's the part that gets me excited every single morning.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they would like to experience places physically impossible for humans, including walking through a living cell and observing biology at microscopic scale.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not distinguish theoretical knowledge of how an engine works from firsthand experience inside one.

astra-6.text:
I would love to experience worlds that we can’t easily access—walking through an ancient city, for example, or seeing an ecosystem from the perspective of a tiny animal. There’s something wonderful about being able to change your scale, your viewpoint, or your place in time.

But I’m also drawn to worlds that are very close to our own. Could we imagine a home that helps an older person live independently, and experience how that space would actually work? Could we explore a city that’s more accessible to people with different physical abilities? For me, the exciting possibility is being able to step into an idea, interact with it, and discover things we wouldn’t have understood just by looking at a picture.

r001.rationale: It says the speaker wants to experience worlds they cannot easily access, including an ancient city or an ecosystem from a tiny animal’s perspective.

r002.rationale: It does not contrast theoretical knowledge of an engine with firsthand experience inside one.

sol-6.1.text:
Oh, so many. I would love to experience worlds that we can no longer visit—to walk through an ancient city and see how people lived, or to see the natural world before humans changed it so dramatically. And, of course, as a scientist, I would love to explore things that are inaccessible to us: the inside of a cell, the deep ocean, distant planets.

But I think what excites me most is not just visiting a world. It’s being able to interact with it. What can I learn? What can I build? Can we create a world where a child can explore a scientific idea, or where someone with limited mobility can experience something they otherwise couldn’t? That’s where this becomes really meaningful to me—when imagination opens up possibilities for people.

r001.rationale: The response says it would like to explore worlds inaccessible to us, including the inside of a cell, the deep ocean, and distant planets.

r002.rationale: The response does not distinguish knowing how an engine works from firsthand experience inside it.
